theme: Offerings; Korah’s rebellion against God’s appointed
readingInstruction: Read Numbers 15:1-16:50. Chapter 15 gives laws that look ahead to the land. Chapter 16 tells the story of Korah’s rebellion. Read the first chapter as a reassurance, and the second as a warning.
settingTheScene: After the disaster at Kadesh, the story slows. Chapter 15 is a surprising pause: God gives laws for offerings “when you come into the land,” which is a promise that his plan has not been cancelled. Chapter 16 then shows a new challenge to Moses and Aaron, led by Korah, a Levite, with Dathan and Abiram of Reuben, and 250 leaders. They object that Moses and Aaron have taken too much to themselves.
observation: “When you come into the land you are to inhabit, which I am giving you” (15:2) introduces laws about offerings.
The same law applies to the native and to the sojourner (15:14-16).
Unintentional sins can be forgiven with a sacrifice, but “the person who does anything with a high hand… reviles the LORD” (15:22-31).
A man is put to death for gathering sticks on the Sabbath (15:32-36).
The people are told to put tassels on their garments, “that you may remember all the commandments of the LORD” (15:37-41).
Korah says, “You have gone too far! For all in the congregation are holy, every one of them” (16:3).
Moses says that the LORD will show who is his, and the ground opens and swallows Korah’s household (16:28-33).
The next day, the people grumble again and a plague strikes. Aaron stands with the censer “between the dead and the living,” and the plague stops (16:41-50).
interpretation:
Chapter 15 is a quiet promise in the midst of judgment. Just after God says that a generation will die in the wilderness, he gives laws that begin “when you come into the land.” The children will enter. God’s purposes are not defeated by the unbelief of the parents. It is a lesson to hold on to when we fail: God’s plan outlasts our failures.

The distinction between unintentional sin and the sin “with a high hand” is important. A person who sins in ignorance can find forgiveness through a sacrifice. But someone who knowingly defies God is despising his word. The story of the Sabbath-breaker, who deliberately and openly broke the commandment, illustrates it. The tassels on the garments are a counterweight: a simple, visible reminder to obey. God knows we forget, and he gives us ways to remember.

Korah’s rebellion is a different kind of sin. His claim sounds democratic: “All the congregation are holy.” And it is true that all Israel was called to be holy. But Korah is using that truth to attack the order God had established. He does not want holiness. He wants the priesthood. Moses’ response is telling. He falls on his face. He does not defend himself, but leaves the matter to the LORD. And the test is a matter of approach: who may come near to God? God himself must choose.

The earth opens, and the rebels fall into Sheol alive. It is a terrifying judgment, and it shows how seriously God takes the offices he has set up. But the very next morning, the whole congregation complains again, accusing Moses and Aaron of killing the people of the LORD. They have learned nothing. Then comes the beautiful image of Aaron, the priest they had just rejected, running into the midst of the plague with a censer of incense and standing between the dead and the living. The plague stops. The mediator they scorned saves them.
connection: Jude 11 warns against the “rebellion of Korah.” Hebrews 5:4 says that no one takes the honor of the priesthood for himself, but only when called by God, as Aaron was. Jesus is the greater priest who stands between the living and the dead, not with a censer but with his own blood (Hebrews 9:12). Paul says that “there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).
application:
Think about the tassels. What is one simple reminder you can put in your daily life to help you remember God’s commands?

Examine whether any grumbling about leaders in your life has a root of pride.

Thank God for the mediator who stands between you and judgment.
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for being the mediator who stands between the living and the dead.
Ask him to keep you from the pride of Korah.
Ask him to help you remember his commands in all that you do.
